sceneFacts.shortVersion: Cooper based Adam Jones on real-life celebrity chefs.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Bradley Cooper based his character Adam Jones on Gordon Ramsay and two other celebrity chefs. Cooper created Adam Jones as a mixture of Marcus Wareing, Gordon Ramsay, and Marco Pierre White, incorporating physical characteristics he "stole" from them into his performance. The story and Cooper’s performance were also heavily influenced by the life and personalities of famous chefs including Mario Batali.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Chef Marcus Wareing trained actors to cook and plate food realistically.
sceneFacts.longDescription: To achieve realism in the kitchen scenes, British chef Marcus Wareing trained the actors of "Burnt" to cook and move like professional chefs. He was present on set during filming to ensure that the food preparation and plating looked and felt like an actual restaurant dinner service. Wareing emphasized that the food should taste, look, and smell right, making the plating more authentic as it was done for real consumption. Sienna Miller, who portrays sous chef Helene, was noted as the most technically proficient cook among the cast, even dedicating her own time to learn techniques in Wareing's kitchen.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Chef Marcus Wareing ensured kitchen authenticity for Burnt.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Chef Marcus Wareing's association with "Burnt" began about seven years before the film's release, when screenwriter Steven Knight first contacted him. Wareing consulted on the film's kitchen design, advising on the layout and equipment, and also developed the menu and food concepts. During filming, he was on set to ensure that everything felt like an actual restaurant dinner service, training actors to cook and move like chefs. Wareing prepared all the recipes for the movie, and all scenes of food preparation were done for real, with genuine chefs as extras.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Bradley Cooper performs a cheeky track on the film's soundtrack.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The official soundtrack for Burnt was released by Lakeshore Records, featuring original score and licensed tracks. It includes songs like Barns Courtney's "Fire" and "It Serves Your Right To Suffer" by The Avener & John Lee Hooker. Lead actor Bradley Cooper also performs a "cheeky micro-track" on the album, titled "Ode to a Sous Vide." This 24-second track is considered an "in-joke for kitchen obsessives" and an "Easter egg for fans."

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Adam Jones's restaurant was filmed at The Langham, London.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The Langham Hotel in London served as a primary filming location for "Burnt." Its restaurant, The Roux at the Landau, was featured throughout the film as Adam Jones's restaurant. To ensure authenticity, a fully functioning kitchen set was built specifically for the movie's kitchen scenes. Michelin-starred chef Marcus Wareing, the film's consultant, prepared all the recipes used in the movie.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: A Michelin chef rated this scene 9/10 for accuracy.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Michelin-starred chef Paul Liebrandt reviewed fine-dining scenes from films, including Adam Jones's pursuit of three Michelin stars in Burnt. Liebrandt rated the scene a near-perfect 9/10 for its accuracy in depicting the pursuit of Michelin stars. He praised the film for accurately capturing the high standards and intense environment of a kitchen striving for these accolades. However, Liebrandt also noted that Burnt simplifies the complex, often years-long process of earning Michelin stars.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Burnt's October release was mandated by company policy.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Distributor Harvey Weinstein believed that Burnt would have performed better with a January release. However, The Weinstein Company's board policies mandated that a certain number of films be released each quarter, which forced Burnt into an October slot.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Burnt's budget was $32.7 million, not the reported $20 million.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The film "Burnt" was reported to have a budget of $20 million, which it eventually earned back within a month of its release. However, records from the Louisiana film commission indicate a higher budget of $32,720,685.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Burnt earned $36M worldwide, but had a tough opening weekend.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Burnt was produced with a budget of $20 million. During its opening weekend, the film earned $5,002,521, which was the fourth worst result on record for a movie released in over 3,000 cinemas. By the end of its theatrical run, the film grossed just over $36 million worldwide.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: Burnt was released as "Super Chef" in some countries.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The film was initially intended to be titled "Chef," but this was changed due to Jon Favreau's movie already using the name. Producers then considered "Adam Jones" for a long time before settling on "Burnt." In some international markets, the film was released under the alternative title "Super Chef."

sceneFacts.shortVersion: "Burnt" originated from a Keanu Reeves idea.
sceneFacts.longDescription: Screenwriter Steven Knight's initial concept for "Burnt" came from a conversation he had with actor Keanu Reeves, who suggested a story about an American chef in London. Knight began developing the screenplay around seven years before the film's release. He was drawn to the kitchen setting due to its "tyranny," where a single person's absolute control creates intense personal dramas.

sceneFacts.shortVersion: The Weinstein Company spent over $20M on Burnt's advertising.
sceneFacts.longDescription: The Weinstein Company invested in a domestic print and advertising (P&A) campaign for Burnt. This included $12.3 million specifically for television ads. The total domestic P&A spend, which also covered print, online, and other fees, exceeded $20 million.
